nota.t: 1.1 Science in daily life
Science is the systematic study of nature through observation and experiment. Fields: biology, chemistry, physics, astronomy, geology.
1.3 Physical quantities and units

A physical quantity is anything that can be measured. The five base quantities and their S.I. units are length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), temperature (kelvin, K) and electric current (ampere, A). Prefixes such as kilo (1 000), centi (0.01) and milli (0.001) make very large or small values easy to write.

t: Prefixes: kilo (k) = 1 000, centi (c) = 0.01, milli (m) = 0.001, micro (µ) = 0.000 001
Accuracy, consistency (precision) and sensitivity of instruments.

nota.t: 1.4 The scientific method

Choose the right instrument: ruler, vernier calipers or micrometer screw gauge for length, a balance for mass, a stopwatch for time and a thermometer for temperature. Accuracy is how close a reading is to the true value, consistency is how close repeated readings are, and sensitivity is how well an instrument detects small changes.

t: Manipulated variable: what you change.
Responding variable: what you observe.
Constant (fixed) variable: what you keep the same.

nota.t: Lab safety: know the hazard symbols, wear a lab coat and goggles, report accidents to the teacher.
1.5 Density and Scientific Investigation

Density is mass per unit volume: density = mass ÷ volume, in g/cm³ or kg/m³. Objects less dense than water (1 g/cm³) float, and denser ones sink. A scientific investigation follows the steps: problem, hypothesis, variables, experiment, data, interpretation and conclusion.

v.c: Liquids and objects in order of density

topik.nama: 2. Cell as the Basic Unit of Life

nota.t: 2.1 Cells: structure and function

The cell is the basic unit of life. Animal and plant cells both have a nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane; plant cells also have a cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts. The nucleus controls the cell, mitochondria release energy and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
The cell is the basic unit of life. Unicellular organisms (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium) and multicellular ones (e.g. humans, trees).

baris: Controls what goes in and out

nota.t: * plant cells only.
2.2 Cell organisation

Cells of the same kind form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems and systems form an organism. Cellular respiration releases energy in mitochondria (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy), while photosynthesis in chloroplasts makes glucose and oxygen using light.
Cell → Tissue → Organ → System → Organism
2.3 Cell respiration and photosynthesis

All living things carry out life processes: respiration, nutrition, excretion, growth, response to stimuli, movement and reproduction. Unicellular organisms such as Amoeba do all of these in one cell; multicellular organisms share the work among specialised cells.

t: Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light, chlorophyll)

nota.t: 3.1 Senses and sense organs
Homeostasis is keeping the internal environment of the body stable. The body controls temperature, water content and blood sugar, so that cells can work properly even when the surroundings change.

v.c: Keeping conditions inside the body steady

t: Long sight: convex lens.
Short sight: concave lens.
Optical illusions and the blind spot show the limits of sight.

nota.t: 3.2 Human responses

When hot, the body sweats and blood vessels in the skin widen to lose heat; when cold, it shivers and the vessels narrow to keep heat. Water balance is kept by the kidneys: more concentrated urine is made when we drink little or sweat a lot.

v.c: How the body controls temperature and water

nota.t: Stimulus → Receptor → Nerves → Brain/spinal cord → Effector → Response
3.3 Plant responses

Plants also keep a steady internal state. They close their stomata on hot, dry days to reduce water loss through transpiration, and open them when water is plentiful for gas exchange and photosynthesis.
Tropisms: phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism, thigmotropism. Nastic movements are non-directional (e.g. the touch-me-not plant folding).
4.1 Sexual and asexual reproduction

Sexual reproduction joins a male and a female gamete, so the offspring differ from their parents. Asexual reproduction needs only one parent: binary fission (Amoeba), budding (yeast), spore formation (fungi) and vegetative reproduction (sweet potato); the offspring are identical to the parent.

t: Asexual: binary fission, budding, spore formation, vegetative reproduction, regeneration.
Sexual: a male and a female gamete fuse → zygote.

nota.t: 4.2–4.4 Human reproductive system
Puberty brings physical changes. The menstrual cycle is about 28 days; ovulation is around day 14. Personal hygiene matters during menstruation.
4.5–4.6 Plant reproduction
Germination needs water, oxygen and warmth, not light.
4.2 The Human Reproductive System

The male reproductive system includes the testes (which make sperm), sperm ducts, glands and urethra. The female system includes the ovaries (which release ova), Fallopian tubes (where fertilisation happens), the uterus (where the foetus grows), the cervix and the vagina.

v.c: Main parts of the female reproductive system

nota.t: 4.3 The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle usually lasts about 28 days. Days 1–5: menstruation, the uterus lining breaks down. Days 6–13: the lining thickens again. Around day 14: ovulation, an ovum is released. Days 15–28: the lining stays thick; without fertilisation the cycle starts again.
4.4 Fertilisation and Pregnancy

Fertilisation takes place in the Fallopian tube when the nucleus of a sperm fuses with the nucleus of an ovum to form a zygote. The zygote divides into an embryo, which implants in the uterus wall. The placenta and umbilical cord carry oxygen and nutrients to the foetus and remove waste.
4.5 Factors in Foetal Development

A foetus develops well when the mother eats a balanced diet, has regular check-ups and avoids smoking, alcohol, drugs and medicine without a doctor's advice. After birth, breast milk gives the baby nutrients and antibodies.

v.c: Factors in foetal and baby development

nota.t: 4.6 Plant Reproduction

Flowers are the reproductive organs of flowering plants. Pollen from the anther is carried to the stigma (pollination) by wind, insects or water. After fertilisation the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit. Plants also reproduce vegetatively from stems, roots or leaves.
5.1 Matter in nature

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Both living and non-living things are made of matter. Matter can be classified by physical properties such as its state, density, melting and boiling points, and whether it conducts heat and electricity.
Matter is anything with mass that takes up space. Light, sound and heat are not matter.
5.2 The three states of matter

Matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving. In a solid the particles are packed closely and vibrate in fixed places; in a liquid they are close but move past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

v.c: Arrangement and movement of particles (see in 3D)

nota.t: Density = mass ÷ volume (g/cm³)
Chemical properties make new substances (burning, rusting); physical ones do not.
5.3 Changes of State

Heating gives particles more kinetic energy, so matter changes state: melting (solid → liquid), boiling and evaporation (liquid → gas) and sublimation (solid → gas). Cooling reverses this: condensation (gas → liquid) and freezing (liquid → solid). The temperature stays constant during melting and boiling.
6.1 Elements, compounds and mixtures

An element is made of only one kind of atom and is arranged in the Periodic Table by proton number. Elements are metals (shiny, ductile, good conductors), non-metals (dull, brittle, insulators) or noble gases (Group 18, unreactive).

t: Element: one kind of atom only (e.g. O, Fe).
Compound: two or more elements joined chemically (e.g. H₂O).
Mixture: mixed physically, can be separated (e.g. air).

nota.t: 6.2 The Periodic Table

A mixture contains two or more substances mixed physically without a chemical reaction, such as air, sea water and porridge. Each part keeps its own properties and can be separated by filtration, evaporation, distillation, chromatography, a magnet or a separating funnel.
Elements are arranged by proton number. Metals on the left, non-metals on the right, noble gases in group 18.
6.3 Separation methods

A compound forms when two or more elements join chemically, for example water (H₂O) and salt (NaCl). Its properties differ from the elements that made it, and it can only be separated by chemical means such as electrolysis.

t: Filtration, evaporation, distillation, chromatography, magnet, crystallisation.

nota.t: 7.1 What air is made of

Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.03% carbon dioxide and 0.97% noble and other gases, plus a varying amount of water vapour. Oxygen is needed for respiration and combustion; carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
7.2 Burning

Combustion is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases heat and light. A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat (the fire triangle); removing any one puts it out. Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion gives soot and carbon monoxide.
The fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and heat. Fire extinguishers remove at least one.
7.3 Air pollution

Air pollution comes from vehicle and factory smoke, open burning and forest fires. It causes haze, acid rain, ozone thinning, global warming and breathing illnesses. It is reduced by public transport, smoke filters, banning open burning and planting trees.

t: Sources: vehicle exhaust, factories, open burning.
Effects: haze, acid rain, greenhouse effect, breathing problems.
Action: share rides, plant trees, control factory emissions.

nota.t: 8.1 Using mirrors

Plane, concave and convex mirrors have many uses. Plane mirrors are used in periscopes and kaleidoscopes; concave mirrors as make-up mirrors and torch reflectors; convex mirrors at road bends and as vehicle side mirrors because they give a wide view.
Light travels straight. Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection; the rays and the normal lie in one plane.

t: Plane mirror image: upright, virtual, same size, laterally inverted, same distance.
Concave mirror: torch. Convex mirror: car side mirror.

nota.t: 8.3 Refraction of light

Dispersion is the splitting of white light into the seven colours of the spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet) by a prism, because each colour bends by a different amount. A rainbow forms when raindrops disperse sunlight.
Light bends when it passes into a medium of different density.
8.4 Dispersion and colour

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium into another of different density. Light entering a denser medium (air → water) bends towards the normal, so a pool looks shallower and a pencil in water looks bent.
Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (ROYGBIV)
8.2 Properties and Reflection of Light

Light travels in straight lines very fast (3 × 10⁸ m/s) and can travel through a vacuum. Opaque objects block light and form shadows. Reflection follows the law: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A plane mirror image is upright, virtual, the same size and laterally inverted.
9.1 Earth's system and structure

The Earth has four linked systems: the geosphere (rock and soil), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living things). Its structure has layers: the crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core.
Layers: crust, mantle, outer core (liquid), inner core (solid). The crust is split into tectonic plates.
9.2 Rocks

Earth processes are endogenic (from inside the Earth: earthquakes, volcanoes, plate movement) or exogenic (at the surface: weathering, erosion, transport and deposition by water, wind and glaciers). Rocks change from one type to another in the rock cycle.

v.c: Processes that shape the Earth's surface

nota.t: 9.3 Geological processes

Geohazards are damaging natural events such as earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, landslides, floods and sinkholes. Their effects are reduced by early warning systems, careful land-use planning and safety education.

v.c: A coast at risk from geohazards

t: Weathering → erosion → deposition.
Disasters: earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, eruptions.

nota.t: 9.4 Earth's resources

The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Geologists use fossils in sedimentary rock and radioactive dating to find the age of rocks. Earth resources such as water, minerals, petroleum and natural gas must be used sustainably.

v.c: A short timeline of Earth's history

nota.t: Groundwater, minerals, oil and natural gas must be managed sustainably.
